title: Getting data in
summary: Data › Get Data reads Tables, CSV files, other workbooks and whole folders. For a CSV, Excel writes three steps for you: Source, Promoted Headers and Changed Type. Check the types it guessed, and read dates with the locale they were written in.
objectives: Import a Table, a CSV file and a sheet from another workbook.
Recognise the Source, Promoted Headers and Changed Type steps.
Fix a type that Changed Type guessed wrong, by replacing its conversion.
Read dates and numbers written in another locale with Change Type › Using Locale.

p: Data › Get Data is one menu for every kind of source. Each one starts the query with a Source step that knows how to read it.
Databases, SharePoint and the web work the same way.
The file’s path is saved in the query: keep files where the query expects them.
Data › Recent Sources reopens the last few.
In real life: exports a CSV every month. Ishaan imports it straight into Power Query.

p: After you pick a file, Excel shows a preview with three choices. Load puts it straight on a sheet. Transform Data opens the editor first. When the data needs any cleaning, choose Transform Data.
File Origin is the text encoding: 65001 (UTF-8) suits most files.
Delimiter: comma for CSV; tab or semicolon for other exports.
You can always come back: double-click the query to edit it.
In real life: clicked Load on day one and spent an hour fixing the sheet by hand. Now it’s Transform Data, every time.

slides.h: Three steps Excel writes for a CSV
p: A CSV import starts with three steps. Source reads the file into columns called Column1, Column2…. Promoted Headers turns the first row into headings. Changed Type guesses each column’s type from the first 200 rows.
Changed Type is a guess: check every column’s type icon.
Text that looks like a number becomes a number.
Dates are read the way your computer writes them.
In real life: turned item code 0101 into 101. Every lookup to the product list failed.

check.q: After a CSV import, which step turns the first row into column headings?
check.explain: Promoted Headers, also called Use First Row as Headers.

slides.h: Fix a wrong guess at its source
p: If Changed Type made a code into a number, the zeros are already gone. Changing the type to Text in a new step gives 101, not 0101. Change the conversion itself: click the type icon and choose Replace current.
Replace current edits the Changed Type step itself.
Add new step converts the already-wrong value.
Codes, PIN codes, phone numbers and GSTINs are Text.
In real life: fixed the item codes once in Changed Type. Every month since, the lookups just work.

p: 05/03/2026 is 5 March in India and 3 May in the US. The billing system exports US-style dates, so Ishaan reads them with Change Type › Using Locale › English (United States).
The locale is the culture the text was written in, not yours.
The step reads `Table.TransformColumnTypes(…, {{"Inv Date", type date}}, "en-US")`.
Numbers too: 1.234,50 is German for 1,234.50.
In real life: once showed sales on 5 March, 6 April and 9 August. They were all in May.

p: Every column has one type, shown by the icon at the left of its heading. Pick the one that matches what the column means.
ABC/123 means “any”: no type yet. Set one.
Types decide what the Excel sheet gets: dates, numbers or text.
The Data Model (Module 6) needs the right types too.
In real life: summed nothing because Amount was text. One click on the type icon fixed it.

frames.say: Data › From Text/CSV › **Transform Data**: Source, Promoted Headers and Changed Type.
Changed Type made **Item Code** a Whole Number: 0101 became 101.
Type icon › **Text** › **Replace current**: the codes keep their zeros.
**Inv Date** with Change Type › Using Locale › Date, **English (United States)**.

lab.intro: Dhanush’s billing system has exported May’s sales as **sales-may-2026.csv**. Import it with Power Query and fix what the automatic steps get wrong. You start in Excel: use the **Data** bar at the top.

cells.A3: Import sales-may-2026.csv with Data › From Text/CSV.

tasks.prompt: Import **sales-may-2026.csv**: Data › From Text/CSV, pick the file, then **Transform Data**.
hints: Click From Text/CSV in the Data bar.
In the preview, click Transform Data.
tasks.solution:
let
    Source = Csv.Document(File.Contents("C:\Data\Dhanush\sales-may-2026.csv"),[Delimiter=",", Columns=6, Encoding=65001, QuoteStyle=QuoteStyle.None]),
    #"Promoted Headers" = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source, [PromoteAllScalars=true]),
    #"Changed Type" = Table.TransformColumnTypes(#"Promoted Headers",{{"Inv No", type text}, {"Inv Date", type text}, {"Branch", type text}, {"Item Code", Int64.Type}, {"Qty", Int64.Type}, {"Amount", type number}})
in
    #"Changed Type"
tasks.explain: Data › From Text/CSV › sales-may-2026.csv › **Transform Data**. Excel writes Source, Promoted Headers and Changed Type.

    Source = Csv.Document(File.Contents("C:\Data\Dhanush\sales-may-2026.csv"),[Delimiter=",", Columns=6, Encoding=65001, QuoteStyle=QuoteStyle.None]),

in
    #"Changed Type"

tasks.prompt: Changed Type made **Item Code** a Whole Number, so 0101 shows as 101. Make it **Text** so the codes keep their leading zeros.
hints: Click the 1²3 icon on the Item Code header and pick Text.
Excel asks: Replace current, or Add new step?
Replace current: a new step can’t bring back zeros that are gone.
tasks.solution:
let
    Source = Csv.Document(File.Contents("C:\Data\Dhanush\sales-may-2026.csv"),[Delimiter=",", Columns=6, Encoding=65001, QuoteStyle=QuoteStyle.None]),
    #"Promoted Headers" = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source, [PromoteAllScalars=true]),
    #"Changed Type" = Table.TransformColumnTypes(#"Promoted Headers",{{"Inv No", type text}, {"Inv Date", type text}, {"Branch", type text}, {"Item Code", type text}, {"Qty", Int64.Type}, {"Amount", type number}})
in
    #"Changed Type"
tasks.explain: Item Code’s type icon › **Text** › **Replace current**. The Changed Type step now reads `{"Item Code", type text}`, so the text is never turned into a number.

tasks.prompt: **Inv Date** is US-style (month/day/year). Make it a **Date**, read with the locale **English (United States)**.

A plain Date would read the day first, as in India.

quiz.explain: Fixed decimal keeps four decimal places exactly.

points: **Get Data** reads Tables, CSV files, workbooks and folders; choose **Transform Data** to clean first.
A CSV starts with **Source**, **Promoted Headers** and **Changed Type**; Changed Type is a guess.
Fix a wrong guess with **Replace current**; read foreign dates with **Change Type › Using Locale**.
recap.cheat: CSV: Source → Promoted Headers → Changed Type; fix wrong types in place; dates need the right locale.

cards.front: Codes lost their leading zeros in Changed Type. The fix?
cards.back: Change the type to **Text** with **Replace current**, not a new step.

cards.front: Read Inv Date as a US-style date

cards.back: **Date order**, the **decimal point** and the **thousands separator** a text was written with.
**Fixed decimal number** ($): four decimal places, exactly.
